code.title: IL bytes of a + b, read back by reflection

followUps: It becomes three or four tiny IL instructions that push both values onto a stack and add them. IL is a stack machine: ldarg.0 pushes a, ldarg.1 pushes b, add pops both and pushes the sum, ret returns the top of the stack. For static int Add(int a, int b) => a + b; the bytes are 02 03 58 2A. The JIT later turns that into something like one lea or add instruction on x64, so the stack never really exists at run time.

Because the first call to each method has to be JIT-compiled, and the first request also loads assemblies, runs static constructors, builds DI containers and warms caches. Example: a 5 ms request may take 300 ms the first time, because hundreds of methods are compiled at Tier0 and many types are initialised. Fixes: ReadyToRun or Native AOT to precompile, a warm-up request or health check before routing traffic, and keeping start-up work small. Later requests reuse the compiled code, so only the first pays.

code.title: Tiered compilation: call counting promotes hot methods

followUps: Because by Tier1 the class has already been initialised, so the JIT can treat the field's current value as a fixed constant. A static readonly bool Enabled = Config.Read(); that is true at Tier1 compile time lets the JIT delete the if (!Enabled) branch entirely, and a readonly object of a sealed type can even have its calls devirtualized. At Tier0 the class may not be initialised yet, so the JIT cannot do this. That is why the pattern is a cheap feature switch, though it is only a good idea if the value never changes after start-up.

It means a short benchmark can measure slow Tier0 code instead of the optimised code users will run. If you time a method 10 times, you probably measure Tier0 (about 30 calls are needed before promotion, plus a 100 ms delay), so results look 2 to 10 times too slow and noisy. Remedies: warm up for enough iterations and time, let BenchmarkDotNet do its pilot and warm-up phases, or set TieredPGO=0/TieredCompilation=false only to study a specific effect. Always report which mode you measured.

Trimming removes code the linker cannot see being used: unused types, methods and whole assemblies from the app and the framework. It starts from your entry points and keeps what is reachable by static analysis. Example: a 70 MB self-contained app can shrink to 15 MB. The risk is code reached only by reflection (string type names, JSON serialisation of types, DI by name); the trimmer cannot see it and may delete it, so you get warnings (IL2026 and similar) and must fix them with source generators, attributes such as DynamicallyAccessedMembers, or root descriptors.

Because typeof(List<>).MakeGenericType(t) creates a new generic instantiation from a runtime value, and Native AOT must compile all code ahead of time, so it does not know which instantiations will be needed. For reference types a shared canonical version of the code exists, but for value types (List<int>) specific native code must be generated, and there is no JIT to do it at run time. If the instantiation was not seen statically, it fails or throws. Fix: use concrete generics the compiler can see, or source generators instead of reflection.

code.title: Object size model: header, MethodTable, fields, padding

followUps: The lock state lives in the object header, the 8 bytes just before the MethodTable pointer. It starts empty. The first lock stores the owning thread id and a recursion count there (a thin lock, no extra allocation). If another thread contends, or you call Wait/Pulse, the runtime allocates a sync block in a side table and stores its index in the header (an inflated lock). The header also holds the cached default hash code, so a locked object may need an inflated lock to hold both. That is why you should lock on a private dedicated object, not on this or a string.

Because every object needs room for the header (8 bytes), the MethodTable pointer (8 bytes), and at least 8 bytes of space after the pointer. That last slot is reserved so the GC can overwrite a dead object with a free-list node when it compacts or sweeps, and node data (size and next pointer) must fit. So 8 + 8 + 8 = 24 bytes even for new object(), which has no fields. A class with one int field is also 24 bytes, because the int fits in the spare 8.

code.title: Struct layout: field order, Pack and Explicit

followUps: A blittable type has the same in-memory representation in managed and unmanaged code, so it can be passed to native code or copied with no conversion. Examples: int, double, byte, and structs or fixed arrays made only of those. Not blittable: bool (4 bytes in native), char (may become 1 byte), and string or any class (needs marshalling). Blittable arrays can be pinned and passed by pointer with no copy, and MemoryMarshal.Cast or Span reinterpretation also requires them (no references inside).

False sharing is when two threads write different variables that sit in the same 64-byte cache line, so the line bounces between cores and both slow down. Padding spreads the hot variables so each gets its own line. Example: four per-thread counters in a long[4] span 32 bytes, so all four share one line; a [StructLayout(LayoutKind.Sequential, Size = 64)] wrapper per counter places each on its own line. Cost: 8 times more memory per counter, so use it only for hot, contended data.

code.title: Inlining-friendly code: the ThrowHelper pattern

followUps: Guarded devirtualization is a PGO optimisation where the JIT guesses the most common concrete type at a virtual call and adds a type check in front of a direct, inlinable call. Pseudocode: if (obj.GetType() == typeof(Dog)) { inlined Dog.Speak } else { obj.Speak() }. Tier0 instrumentation records which types it saw, so Tier1 can use that. If 95% of calls are Dog, they run fast and branch-predicted, and the rare cases still work through the normal virtual call. It needs dynamic PGO, which is on by default since .NET 8.

Because a sealed class has no subclasses, so a call on it can only reach one method and the JIT can call it directly (and inline it) without a vtable lookup. If Dog is not sealed, d.Speak() might actually run Puppy.Speak(), so a virtual call is required. Sealing is a free hint and also makes type checks like o is Dog a single pointer compare. Seal classes you do not design for inheritance; the benefit is usually small but real in hot paths, and the BCL seals many types for this reason.

code.title: Loops and checks the JIT can prove in range

followUps: Because a field can change between reads, the JIT must assume the array could be replaced, so it cannot reuse one length check. A local variable cannot be changed by other code (except by this method), so the JIT can prove the relation between index and length. Example: for (i = 0; i < this.arr.Length; i++) sum += this.arr[i]; reloads and re-checks each time, while var a = this.arr; for (i = 0; i < a.Length; i++) sum += a[i]; has no bounds check. It is also faster because the array reference stays in a register.

Loop cloning makes two copies of a loop: a fast one with no bounds checks, and the original slow one. Before the loop, the JIT inserts a check that proves all indexes will be in range (for example, that n <= a.Length). If the check passes, the fast copy runs; if not, the slow copy runs and throws at the right point. Example: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) s += a[i]; where n is unrelated to a.Length gets one check up front instead of n checks. The cost is bigger code size, so the JIT only does it for hot loops.

code.title: Mini benchmark harness: warm-up, repeats, median

followUps: Because a Stopwatch loop measures one cold, uncontrolled run: it includes JIT time, Tier0 code, CPU frequency changes and noise, and the JIT may delete code whose result is unused. A loop of 1000 calls may report 50 ms of mostly JIT warm-up, while the real steady state is 5 ms. BenchmarkDotNet handles warm-up, picks iteration counts, runs in a separate process, removes outliers, and reports statistics. A Stopwatch is fine for rough checks, but only after warm-up, with repeated runs, median results, and the result consumed.

A large StdDev (relative to the Mean, say over 10%) suggests the measurement is unstable or the code has variable cost. Typical causes: GC pauses inside the measured code, other processes on the machine, thermal throttling or CPU frequency scaling, tiering changing mid-run, data-dependent branches, or a few slow outliers such as cache misses. Check Min, Median and Max, rerun on a quiet machine, and look at the allocation column. A bimodal distribution (two clusters) often points to a GC or tiering transition.

code.title: Hidden allocations: boxing, ArrayList and closures

followUps: A static lambda (C# 9: static x => x + 1) cannot capture locals or this, so the compiler can cache it as a single delegate object that is created once and reused. A lambda that captures a variable allocates a closure object and a new delegate on every execution of the enclosing code. Example: list.Sort(static (a, b) => a.Id - b.Id) allocates nothing per call, while capturing threshold allocates 2 objects. The static keyword also makes the compiler error if you accidentally capture something.

ValueTask<T> is worth it when the method completes synchronously most of the time, such as a cache hit, a buffered read or a pooled result. A Task<T> allocates a heap object (about 72 bytes) for every call even when the result is ready, but a ValueTask<T> returned from a synchronous path allocates nothing. If it usually completes asynchronously, there is no saving, and ValueTask has restrictions: await it once only, do not await it twice or concurrently, and call AsTask() to store it. Measure before changing public APIs.

code.title: Parsing a CSV line with no allocations

followUps: The main risks are bugs around ownership: returning a buffer twice, using it after returning it, and leaking data. If you return an array and keep using it, another caller may rent the same array and both write to it. Rented arrays may be larger than requested and contain old data, so use only the length you asked for and clear sensitive data (clearArray: true). Always return in a finally block. Also, a pool that is never trimmed can hold memory, and arrays that escape (stored in fields) are never returned, so the pool just allocates new ones.

System.IO.Pipelines gives you a pooled, reusable buffer between a producer (socket read) and a consumer (parser), so parsing works directly on the received bytes with no copies and no per-message allocations. The reader returns a ReadOnlySequence<byte> that may span several buffer segments; you parse what is complete, then call AdvanceTo(consumed, examined) so the unfinished part stays for the next read. Kestrel uses it. It also handles back-pressure, so a fast sender cannot fill memory.

code.title: String interning and reference equality

followUps: Use your own small dictionary while parsing: look up each new string and reuse the first instance you stored. Example: var pool = new Dictionary<string,string>(); if (!pool.TryGetValue(s, out var p)) pool[s] = p = s; so 1 million rows with 50 distinct countries keep 50 strings instead of 1 million. Better, look up with a span (GetAlternateLookup<ReadOnlySpan<char>> in .NET 9) to avoid creating the string at all. Prefer this over string.Intern, because the pool can be dropped afterwards and the global intern pool never shrinks.

string.IsInterned(s) returns the pooled instance if a string equal to s is already in the intern pool, and returns null if not. Unlike string.Intern, it never adds anything. Example: after string.Intern("abc"), IsInterned(new string(new[]{'a','b','c'})) returns the pooled "abc" object, but IsInterned("never-seen" + x) returns null. It is useful to check without growing the pool.

code.title: Allocation rate drives GC counts

followUps: The mid-life crisis is when objects live just long enough to be promoted to gen1 or gen2 and then die, so the GC pays for expensive higher-generation collections instead of cheap gen0 ones. Example: per-request objects that wait for a 200 ms database call while gen0 collects every 20 ms get promoted, then die in gen2. Gen2 collections are far more costly because they scan the whole heap. Fixes: shorten lifetimes, avoid holding references across slow awaits, pool objects, and avoid caching things with short life spans.

Workstation GC uses one heap and, by default, runs concurrently with a background thread; it prefers low memory and short pauses and suits desktop apps and small containers. Server GC creates one heap and one dedicated GC thread per logical core, so collections run in parallel and throughput is higher, but memory use is larger and each GC uses all cores. Choose Server GC for busy multi-core services focused on throughput. In containers with small memory limits, test both, and in .NET 8 consider DATAS, which adapts the heap count to the load.

Check the result is used: if the benchmark computes a value and throws it away, the JIT may delete the whole computation, giving results like 0.2 ns per op. Signs: time is far lower than one memory access or one CPU cycle would take, time does not grow with the input size, and the disassembly (DisassemblyDiagnoser) has no loop. Fix: return the value from the benchmark method or write it to a field, and use inputs created in [GlobalSetup] instead of constants, which can be folded at compile time.

A performance regression test checks that a key metric does not get worse after a change, using a threshold. Options: a BenchmarkDotNet run in CI compared against saved baselines with an allowed margin (for example, fail if more than 10% slower), or an allocation test asserting GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() delta equals 0. Allocation counts are deterministic, so they make the most stable tests; timings on shared CI machines are noisy, so use ratios against a baseline in the same run and run the check several times.

code.title: False sharing: adjacent vs padded counters

followUps: The cache line is 64 bytes on most x64 CPUs, but some Intel CPUs fetch two adjacent lines at once (the spatial prefetcher pulls in a 128-byte pair). Then two variables 64 bytes apart can still interfere, because writing one invalidates the neighbouring line too. Padding to 128 bytes keeps hot variables in separate pairs. Apple M-series chips also use 128-byte lines. The cost is memory, so use it only for few, heavily written variables such as queue head and tail indexes.

Look for a mismatch between expected and measured speed: a multi-threaded loop on separate variables that is slower than one thread, or does not scale as threads are added. Then confirm with hardware counters: on Linux perf c2c reports cache lines with contended writes, and Intel VTune has a false-sharing analysis. A quick experiment is to add 64 or 128 bytes of padding between the variables and see if the speed jumps (say from 4 s to 0.5 s). If it does, you found it.

code.title: Struct dictionary keys: IEquatable avoids boxing

followUps: HashCode.Combine(a, b, c) mixes the hash codes of its arguments into one int that depends on all of them and on their order. It starts from a random seed (generated once per process), so values change between runs, which stops attackers from crafting colliding keys. Example: HashCode.Combine(X, Y) gives different results for (1, 2) and (2, 1), unlike X ^ Y, which gives 3 for both. It supports up to 8 values; for more, use a HashCode instance with Add. Never save these values to disk.

Because a dictionary uses the hash code to pick a bucket, and only compares keys inside that bucket. If two equal keys have different hashes, they land in different buckets and the lookup never finds the stored one, even though Equals says they match. Example: Key(1,2) hashed by reference returns 17 once and 42 the next time, so dict[Key(1,2)] throws KeyNotFoundException. The reverse is allowed: different keys may share a hash (a collision), which is only slower. So whatever Equals compares, GetHashCode must use the same fields.
